title: DIG FAST

sections.collegeNotes:
Memory hook for the seven criterion B symptoms of a manic/hypomanic episode. Criterion A (elevated/expansive/irritable mood plus increased energy/activity) is not in the letters and must be present first.

### D — Distractibility

Attention too easily drawn to unimportant or irrelevant external stimuli

Attention is too easily drawn to unimportant external stimuli (commenting on wallpaper mid-conversation, starting three tasks and finishing none). A DSM-5 criterion B symptom of mania/hypomania.

**Physiology.** Hyper-aroused, poorly filtered brain: elevated dopamine/norepinephrine reduces attentional control, so salient-but-irrelevant cues pull the spotlight of attention.

**Safety.** Minimize environmental stimulation and give one simple instruction at a time to reduce escalation.

### I — Indiscretion / risky behavior

Excessive involvement in pleasurable activities with high potential for painful consequences

Excessive involvement in pleasurable activities with high potential for painful consequences: spending sprees, reckless driving, gambling, foolish investments, sexual indiscretions. Uncharacteristic and can cause financial, legal, or relationship harm.

**Physiology.** Reduced frontal (executive) control over reward-driven behavior, so immediate reward wins over long-term consequences.

**Safety.** Can be immediately dangerous (reckless driving, unsafe sex, large financial loss); document and involve family, and limit access to funds/credit during acute mania.

### G — Grandiosity

Inflated self-esteem or grandiosity

Inflated self-esteem or grandiosity, ranging from unrealistic sense of one's abilities to delusions of grandeur (special powers, immense wealth, divine mission) in mania with psychotic features. Strikingly out of proportion to circumstances.

**Physiology.** Reduced self-monitoring and exaggerated reward signaling produce overconfident self-appraisal that ignores limits and feedback.

**Safety.** Do not argue with grandiose beliefs; acknowledge the feeling, stay calm and firm, and set limits on unsafe behavior.

### F — Flight of ideas

Racing thoughts; speech that shifts abruptly between loosely connected topics

Subjective report of racing thoughts and/or rapid speech that shifts abruptly between loosely connected topics (by rhyme, pun, or distractible associations). If connections are lost entirely, it may be loosening of associations (more characteristic of psychosis).

**Physiology.** Accelerated thought processes outpace the capacity to organize them, producing rapid, tangential verbal output from a hyperactive associative network.

**Safety.** Document rate and coherence of speech; structure the interview with closed questions.

### A — Activity increase

Increased goal-directed activity or psychomotor agitation

Increase in goal-directed activity (work, school, social, sexual) or psychomotor agitation (pacing, hand-wringing). DSM-5 requires increased activity/energy (with mood) as part of criterion A, underscoring its importance.

**Physiology.** Heightened dopaminergic/noradrenergic drive increases energy and motor output; reduced frontal control makes the energy poorly organized.

**Safety.** Channel energy safely (walking, non-competitive activities) and protect from exhaustion and injury.

### S — Sleep deficit (decreased need for sleep)

Feels rested after only ~3 hours of sleep

Decreased need for sleep (feeling rested after ~3 hours) is one of the most specific symptoms of mania and an early warning sign. Distinct from insomnia, where the person wants to sleep but cannot and feels tired the next day.

**Physiology.** Arousal systems are 'stuck on,' suppressing the normal drive and perception of needing sleep.

**Safety.** A key clue distinguishing mania from depression/anxiety; prioritize sleep restoration as part of treatment.

### T — Talkativeness (pressure of speech)

More talkative than usual; pressure to keep talking

More talkative than usual or a pressure to keep talking — rapid, forceful, difficult-to-interrupt speech (pressured speech). Combined with flight of ideas, gives the classic pressured, tangential speech of mania.

**Physiology.** Accelerated thought production plus reduced inhibition produces fast, abundant verbal output that 'leaks' the racing thoughts.

**Safety.** Listen briefly to build rapport, then structure the interview with closed questions; do not compete verbally.

sections.eli10:
A pocket checklist for the 'too fast, too high, too big' state of mania, so you can tell the difference between 'cheerful' and 'unwell.'

**D — Distractibility.** Like trying to listen to one person while ten radios play at once — attention keeps jumping to every new sound because the brain can't ignore background noise.

**I — Indiscretion / risky behavior.** The brain's 'pause button' is broken, so the person acts on impulse without thinking about consequences — like buying a car they can't afford.

**G — Grandiosity.** Thinking you are much bigger, better, or more important than you really are — the 'you're great!' switch is stuck all the way up.

**F — Flight of ideas.** Thoughts zoom so fast they crash into each other, and the person jumps from one idea to the next like a train going too fast to stay on the tracks.

**A — Activity increase.** The 'go' pedal is floored — the person is constantly doing things, starting many projects at once and finishing none, or pacing and fidgeting nonstop.

**S — Sleep deficit (decreased need for sleep).** Different from 'can't sleep': the person sleeps only a few hours and feels full of energy, not tired — like the body forgot it needs rest.

**T — Talkativeness (pressure of speech).** The words pour out fast and it's hard to interrupt — a fire hose of words the person can't turn off.
